summary: The note surveys modern efforts to combat the tobacco epidemic, starting with WHO and CDC death and cost statistics. It then describes campaigns from late 2023 to early 2024, covering social media analytics, a quit-support app, grassroots community programs, policy and tax changes, and school education. It ends with how success is measured and a heading on economic incentives that has no content.
one_line: Overview of tobacco death and cost statistics and the outreach, community, policy and education campaigns launched in 2023-2024 to reduce tobacco use.
key_facts: The WHO says tobacco kills more than 8 million people each year, with around 1.2 million of those deaths from non-smokers exposed to secondhand smoke.
The CDC reports cigarette smoking causes more than 480,000 deaths per year in the United States, including more than 41,000 from secondhand smoke exposure.
The global economy loses more than $1 trillion annually to tobacco-related healthcare expenses and lost productivity.

On October 15, 2023, Dr. Elizabeth Torres introduced a campaign using social media analytics from platforms like Instagram and Twitter to reach young adults at risk of starting to smoke; preliminary studies show a 5% decrease in tobacco initiation among the targeted demographic.

On November 3, 2023, a non-profit led by former smoker Michael Lin launched an app offering personalized quit support that uses machine learning to predict and intervene when a user is most likely to relapse.

On December 10, 2023, a grassroots program was created in Springfield by local health professionals including Dr. Karen Simmons, with town hall meetings, workshops and mobile clinics offering free screenings, cessation aids and counseling.
Early results from the Springfield program suggest a 12% increase in successful quit rates compared to the previous year.
On January 5, 2024, the federal government passed a bill raising the tobacco purchasing age to 21 nationwide.
A significant tobacco tax increase on January 15, 2024 led to a reported 3% decline in tobacco product sales in the first quarter of the year.

Starting February 20, 2024, the Department of Health ran a nationwide education campaign with Prof. Anthony Rivera, including a school curriculum, public service announcements and sessions for parents and caregivers.
The school curriculum is interactive, with modules simulating the consequences of tobacco addiction over a lifetime.

Success is tracked through surveillance of smoking prevalence, number of smokers who quit and reduced hospital admissions, with findings analyzed by officials such as Jonathon Pierce, head of the National Tobacco Control Program.
